cards.title: Static Ads as the Cheapest Creative Testing Ground
cards.summary: Statics cost far less to produce and serve than video, making them the fastest, cheapest way to test new angles, offers and personas before investing in video production.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to allocate creative production budget for testing new product angles, offers or personas in a paid social account.
steps: Recognize the production math the source cites: in the time needed to produce one 60-90 second video, you can produce roughly three to four statics, and AI-assisted statics can cost around a dollar each.
Use statics as the first test of any new angle, offer, persona or product before committing to higher-cost video shoots.
Run offer split tests directly in statics on warm audiences to learn which offer converts best and what gross profit it returns.
When a static concept performs, roll that winning concept into a higher-production video rather than starting video ideation blind.

Account for the caveat that statics tend to convert lower in the funnel than video, so make the deliberate effort to build statics that sit higher in the stages of awareness rather than only making retargeting ads.
caveats: Static ads have the lowest CPMs and generally beat video unless there is a compliance issue; this is the source's claim and may vary by account and platform.
The 4x production cost figure and $1-per-static AI cost are source estimates, not guaranteed benchmarks.

cards.title: Clarity vs Curiosity: Never Sit in the Middle
cards.summary: Static ads must be either maximally clear about the offer or deliberately curiosity-driven; ads that mix both fail as undifferentiated 'slop' and get stuck as mid-funnel attribution-scoopers.
cards.use_when: Reviewing or briefing a static ad creative to decide whether its messaging direction is decisive enough to perform on cold audiences.
steps: Before building, decide which pole the static sits at: maximum clarity (viewer understands the offer, angle and audience within 3-4 seconds) or a deliberate curiosity gap (viewer has no idea what is being sold and clicks to find out).
For the clarity pole, make the problem being agitated, the solution and the offer explicit in the image plus primary text.
For the curiosity pole, withhold the offer in the image and let the primary text or landing page close the gap.
Review each finished static against a specific question: is this ad clear enough to sell, or curious enough to pull a click? If it is neither, rework it rather than running it.
Note that clear ads use long-form copy and native formats to move viewers through awareness stages, and curiosity ads use educational or advertorial landing pages to complete the conversion.
Accept that the middle-ground ad will sit as a mid/bottom-funnel ad, scoop up attribution, and never be turned off but also never drive growth.
caveats: A middle-ground static is not automatically worthless; the source frames it as a common failure mode that lacks upside, not a compliance risk.

cards.title: Avoid Last-Click Attribution on Top-of-Funnel Statics
cards.summary: Top-of-funnel static ads drive cheap clicks and halo conversions that retargeting ads claim under last-click attribution, so judging them by in-platform ROAS alone wrongly kills them.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether to scale or kill top-of-funnel static ads, or setting up creative reporting that reflects true business contribution.
steps: Expect top-of-funnel curiosity statics to show cheap CPCs and heavy traffic that later gets retargeted and converted by middle- and bottom-funnel creative.
Do not kill a top-of-funnel static just because its in-platform ROAS is below your bottom-of-funnel statics' ROAS.
Measure success and scale against financial KPIs (blended revenue, gross profit, new-customer volume) rather than in-platform last-click ROAS alone.
Use long-form landing pages (advertorials, quizzes) on top-of-funnel creatives so the pre-education happens on-site rather than relying on the ad to sell alone.
Where possible, examine account-level and new-customer trends around the period the top-of-funnel static is live.
Treat any single-platform metric as incomplete evidence; combine it with the halo effect on the rest of the account.
caveats: The source presents this as a major reason static ads appear not to work; attribution approaches vary by platform and store, so verify current attribution settings.
This does not mean bottom-of-funnel statics should be exempt from ROAS scrutiny; both funnel roles have different success bars.

cards.title: Concept = Persona × Angle × Offer (not design)
cards.summary: A true creative concept changes the persona, angle or offer; design tweaks and format swaps alone are just variations and do not broaden reach.
cards.use_when: Briefing a creative team or reviewing submitted statics to confirm whether they represent genuinely new concepts or just cosmetic variations.
steps: Define a concept as the combination of target persona, angle and offer (format is optional and secondary).
Treat three new statics as variations unless one of persona, angle or offer has changed; a new product or a different value representation counts as a new offer.
Examples of changing angle on the same product: weight-loss framing versus longevity framing.
Examples of changing persona: women aged 30-40 versus men; the same format and offer can rotate personas to reach new audiences.
Instruct designers not to count a new design or template as a new concept; describe concepts in words so the strategist and designer share language.
When a format works, scale it by substituting one concept element (persona, offer, angle) while retaining the same format and messaging structure.
caveats: Format is optional in the concept framework; the source explicitly removes it when the discussion is constrained to static images.

cards.title: Ad Volume Forecasting: Churn Back-Propagation
cards.summary: Back-calculate required static ad volume from how fast winning ads churn and your historical hit rate, rather than testing as much as possible.
cards.use_when: Planning monthly creative output or deciding how many new static ads to produce to sustain paid social performance.
steps: Count current winning ads in the account (e.g., 10 winners this month).
Measure how many winners churn per month to get a churn rate (e.g., 2 of 10 = 20%).
Determine your winning hit rate from historical account data; the source cites 5-15% as normal for large accounts.
Divide the churn replacement requirement by the hit rate to get required volume: 2 winners to replace at 5% hit rate means 40 ads per month, assuming quality stays consistent.

Alternatively, back-propagate from average revenue per ad: average spend per ad, average ROI, average revenue per ad unit, and average ad duration, then solve for the ad count needed to hit a revenue target.
Use both models together as the source does; the source presents 5-15% hit rate and 5% (20 ads per winner) as heuristics, not universal benchmarks.
caveats: Hit rate and churn vary by account, category and creative quality; 5-15% and '40 ads for 2 replacements' are illustrative source examples, not promises.
Do not simply test as much as possible; you need enough budget behind ads to reach statistical relevance.

cards.title: Prioritize Research Over Concepting Over Production
cards.summary: The static ad production pipeline is research → concepting → build → variations → feedback, and quality collapses if you skip straight to design tools like Canva.
cards.use_when: Structuring a static ad production workflow or diagnosing why existing statics underperform despite good design.
steps: Do not open Canva or a template library first; start in a word document or research tool.
Spend roughly 80% of effort on research and concepting, per the source's guidance.
Research means genuinely understanding the consumer, their pain points and their language, not assuming you already know them.
Concept (define persona, angle, offer) only after research is done, then build the static, then vary, then get feedback and launch.
Use AI selectively rather than fully automating every stage; the source recommends human intervention at research or concepting even if build and variations are AI-assisted.
Have AI assist research by scraping large datasets, but keep concepting human because LLM concepting produces the same ideas across everyone.
Recognize that AI struggles to cross-translate peripheral ideas from other industries, which is where human creative differentiation and arbitrage come from.
caveats: The 80% figure is the source's recommendation for effort allocation, not a measured finding.
The source notes AI can be used at every stage but warns that automating everything produces slop creative.

cards.title: Creative Variation: Change One Concept Element, Not the Pixel
cards.summary: Because Meta's Andromeda groups near-identical ads, tiny design changes have no measurable uplift; variations should change persona, offer or angle while keeping the winning format.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to change when scaling a winning static format, or rejecting a designer's background-color variations.
steps: Define a real variation as a material change to persona, offer or angle; a background color swap or slightly different product pose is not worth testing.
Understand that a color change might produce a 1-2% delta that is statistically unmeasurable without enormous budgets, which the source calls a bad use of spend.
Run tests that are measurable, get meaningful spend behind them, and materially change future creative direction (feeding a creative flywheel).
Treat extremely small variations as wasted because Andromeda will natively group similar ads under the same ad ID and serve them to the same audience.
When scaling a format, substitute a concept element: keep the format and messaging, but swap the product (e.g., greens powder to protein powder) or the persona while holding offer and angle constant.
Use variations only to squeeze a bit more spend through an already-proven concept, not to test whether that concept works.
caveats: The source claims Meta introduced this grouping to counter AI-driven ad volume; verify current platform behavior as it may change.
This does not mean format innovation is worthless; a genuinely new format can create temporary first-mover arbitrage.

cards.title: Expected Gross Profit Per Ad: The Real Comparison Metric
cards.summary: Compare creative types by expected gross profit after production cost (revenue per ad minus ad spend minus production cost), not by headline ROAS alone.
cards.use_when: Choosing between producing more statics or more videos in a paid social budget, or justifying a static-heavy creative plan.
steps: Calculate average revenue per ad unit for each creative type in the account.
Subtract average ad spend per ad (based on the account's actual return, not an idealized one).
Subtract the production cost per ad for that creative type (statics roughly $20, video roughly $200 per the source's example).
Compare the resulting gross profit per ad; the source's illustration shows statics at $880 versus video at $700 at 10x return, and $480 versus $300 at 2x return.
At lower returns, the production-cost gap widens the gross profit difference between cheap and expensive creative.
Use this calculation to prioritize statics for testing and to justify shifting budget toward cheaper creative in lower-ROAS scenarios.
caveats: All figures ($1,000 revenue, 10x/2x return, $20/$200 costs) are the source's illustrative examples, not promised outcomes.
ROAS, ad spend and production costs vary widely; plug in your own account numbers.

cards.title: Stages of Awareness Applied to Static Ads
cards.summary: Static ads tend to sit low in the stages of awareness; to scale them you must deliberately build statics for higher awareness stages and use primary text plus landing pages to bridge the gap.
cards.use_when: Choosing what awareness level a new static ad should target, especially when trying to reach cold audiences instead of retargeting buyers.
steps: Identify where a proposed static sits on the awareness spectrum: unaware, problem aware, solution aware or most aware.
Recognize the most-aware product-shot static only resonates with people who already know the product and likely visited the site; this is the style 90% of people default to, per the source.
Build solution-aware statics for cold audiences (people who know the problem but not your product).
Place 'problem aware' work higher up the funnel and consider it very cold.
For unaware audiences, use the static image to redirect attention into long-form primary text or an educational landing page; a 4-second static alone cannot teach a problem, a solution and a product.
Pair each static with copy and a landing page at the same stage; mismatched copy and image (e.g., a product-aware image with solution-aware copy) kills performance.
caveats: Static ads cannot easily communicate across all awareness stages within one 1080x1080 image; this is a structural limitation, not a design failure.
The '90% of statics' figure is the source's assertion about common practice, not a measured statistic.

cards.title: Design the Visual Hierarchy on Three Levers
cards.summary: Control how a viewer's eye moves through a static using sizing, contrast and whitespace so the first fixation lands on the highest-awareness element.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a static ad layout, or briefing a designer on how the eye should travel through the creative.
steps: Identify where the viewer's eye lands first (the largest, highest-contrast element) and make sure that element carries the highest-awareness message, not 'protein powder' when it could be 'new technology'.
Recall that sizing directs the eye to the largest element, contrast directs it to whatever differs most, and whitespace redirects attention away from empty space onto the meaningful elements.
Lead the eye through the static in a sequence that pulls the viewer up or through the stages of awareness: high-awareness hook first, then image that creates intrigue, then resolution.
Use the example of a folded powder product: the first headline 'new technology' pulls a broad audience, the clear protein mixing image creates confusion, and subsequent elements resolve it.
Understand that pure design quality is secondary to message clarity, but bad design can destroy authority built by other elements (e.g., poor spacing, off-center product).
Note that design matters most when the static must be non-native and clickbaity, or when it needs to compress an angle, offer and audience into very few words.
caveats: The source argues design is not the skill in a static; clarity, messaging and copywriting matter more. Design still matters for framing and authority.

cards.title: Treat Primary Text and Headline as Core, Not Decoration
cards.summary: On statics, headlines and primary text get far more consumption than on video, so build a YouTube-thumbnail-style curiosity pairing between image and text.
cards.use_when: Writing the copy that accompanies a static ad image, or reviewing primary text in a static ad breakdown.
steps: Treat the headline and primary text as equally weighted with the image on statics, because viewers are more likely to read both than on a video ad.

Build a curiosity pairing between image and text like a YouTube thumbnail and title: image raises a question ('what is this mystery powder?'), text adds context without fully resolving it, and the click resolves it.
For native-style statics, keep the image vague (e.g., blurred product) and let the primary text carry the selling.

Check whether the copy matches the awareness stage of the image; a product-aware image paired with solution-aware copy (e.g., a creatine product shot with copy explaining what creatine is) will not work.
For ads with very little text in the image, use long-form primary text to walk the viewer through awareness stages.
Ensure the CTA and primary text support the direction the image set: clickbaity or advertorial images drive a click, native images rely on copy to pull the reader through.
caveats: This applies primarily to statics; the source says headline/primary-text consumption is much lower on video ads.
Copy alone cannot rescue a static whose image sits at a mismatched awareness stage.

cards.title: Native vs Non-Native Scroll-Stop Levers
cards.summary: Statics stop the scroll either by feeling native to the platform or by being deliberately non-native and clickbaity; each direction dictates where the message and selling live.
cards.use_when: Deciding the creative direction (native organic-feel vs. obvious ad) for a new static before starting design.
steps: Choose the native route: mimic organic platform content (notepad, text-message, tweet-style formats) so viewers do not register the ad; familiarity stops the scroll and the format gives room to communicate the message.
Choose the interrupt route: make the static dramatically non-native and clickbaity so it is a pattern interrupt; this drives cheap clicks to educational landing pages.
For native statics, plan to carry the selling in long-form primary text and a landing page, since the image gives little away and may not even be recognized as an ad.

For clickbaity or advertorial statics, drive to an educational lander (advertorial, listicle, quiz) rather than a standard product page; do not try to sell directly on the landing page in that direction.
Innovate on format when possible: copied formats only help if you are first to market, but a new working format gives temporary arbitrage.
caveats: Model-based native formats can carry brand-safety and legal risk; the source notes blurring brand-identifiable packaging may be advisable but is not certain.
A native static that feels organic still needs the primary text and landing page to do the selling.

cards.title: Whitelisting/Native Static with Long-Form Copy (IM8 Example)
cards.summary: A tweet-style static run from a personality profile, agitating a very wide symptom list and educating on solutions, can reach cold audiences without looking like an ad.
cards.use_when: Planning a native or whitelisting-style static around a broad symptom/problem list for a supplement or wellness product.
steps: Run the static from a personality or partner profile (not a brand collaboration) so it feels like organic content and reaches that person's audience.
Lead with a broad problem-agitation list addressed to a very wide audience (e.g., dry eyes, poor vision, low energy, bad skin, fatigue, bleeding gums, painful muscles) to maximize addressable market.
Educate on what each symptom might indicate (e.g., which vitamin deficiency maps to which symptom), then introduce the product as the resolving solution.
Maintain the organic feel by not attaching the brand name to the post.
Keep the primary text long-form, moving the reader from problem to education to product to CTA.
Understand that this static, with a curiosity-building image and hooking long-form copy, typically works well for cold traffic, per the source.
caveats: The source calls this its own observation of a live competitor ad, not a guaranteed template.
Whitelisting and personality-page ads carry platform and disclosure considerations; verify current rules.

cards.title: Long-Copy Story Static for Older/Problem-Aware Audiences
cards.summary: A plain, organic-looking story post with a long narrative about a personal problem can pull a wide audience and disqualify non-relevant viewers through its content.
cards.use_when: Writing a static ad aimed at an older or problem-aware audience (e.g., menopause, hormonal issues) that needs trust built through story.
steps: Write the static as if it were an organic Facebook post from an individual, not a brand, to reduce ad recognition.
Open with a line that broadens the audience and creates a mild mystery, then reveal the real topic through the narrative.
Structure the narrative as: protagonist's problem (often affecting relationships), a skeptical attempt at a solution, a 90-day guarantee that lowered the barrier, then the positive outcome.
Use the story to disqualify irrelevant viewers naturally (someone not in the target demographic will scroll past), pre-qualifying the remaining audience.
Explain where the product was found inside the story rather than as a hard sales block.
Follow through to a landing page that matches the story's promised product.
caveats: The source shows this as a strong example, not a universal rule; long narrative copy works best with the right audience and offer.
Do not fabricate specific results; the story format is the transferable part, not any claimed outcome.

cards.title: How Design Quality Conveys or Destroys Authority
cards.summary: Design alone does not sell, but bad spacing and off-center product shots can erase the authority that specificity and positioning build.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a finished static for layout quality before it goes live, or deciding whether to fix design versus rewrite copy.
steps: Check whether design supports or undercuts the authority claims (e.g., a bold specific percentage at the top signals clinical evidence; clunky spacing below it can lose that framing).
Fix basic composition issues: product off-center, poor spacing, inconsistent alignment.
Remove elements that do not earn their space; the source suggests dropping the logo from the static because the brand is visible at the page level.
Replace generic slogans ('you don't have to feel ready, you just have to begin') with concrete features or a review that gives a reason to buy.
Understand that design is not the skill of a static; the messaging, clarity and copywriting are, so do not over-invest in design polish at the expense of the concept.
Use design mainly to control the visual hierarchy and frame, not as a standalone performance lever.
caveats: The source's stance is that design 'really doesn't matter' compared to messaging, but also acknowledges design can erode authority—so fix obvious layout problems even if design is secondary.

cards.title: Match Image and Copy at the Same Awareness Stage
cards.summary: When the static image assumes one awareness stage and the copy speaks to another, the ad fails; the image and copy must sit at the same stage.
cards.use_when: Auditing an existing static ad that is underperforming, or QA review before launch.
steps: Identify the awareness stage the static image assumes (e.g., a product shot means the viewer already knows the product).
Read the primary text and confirm it addresses the same audience; a product-aware image paired with solution-aware copy ('creatine helps you gain strength') will not convert.
When mismatch is found, correct either the image (to match the copy's stage) or the copy (to match the image's stage).
Use a story-based or agitate-based image with copy that speaks to the same problem and audience.
This diagnosis applies to video as well as static: the ad creative and the copy must align to avoid wasted spend.
caveats: The creatine example is the source's illustration; stage definitions come from Eugene Schwartz's awareness model referenced by the source.

cards.title: Rotate Concept Elements to Scale a Winning Format
cards.summary: Once a static format proves out, scale it by substituting a concept element (persona, offer or angle) rather than iterating on the format itself.
cards.use_when: Planning the next batch of statics after a format like problem-agitation or native advertorial has proven to work.
steps: Confirm the format is working (e.g., problem agitation, native static, founder static).
Keep the format and messaging structure constant and swap the product (e.g., apply the greens powder static to the protein powder).
Alternatively, keep format, offer and angle and change the persona addressed (e.g., women 30-40 to men).
Alternatively, keep format and persona and change the angle (e.g., weight-loss framing to longevity framing).
Rotate only one element at a time so you can attribute any performance shift to the change.
Avoid the trap of making endless small format tweaks to a single ad; that yields no meaningful new reach or learning.
caveats: This is the source's recommended scaling method and assumes the base format retains its performance; results depend on the account and audience.
It does not replace the need to still find new winning concepts, only to multiply the reach of existing ones.

cards.title: Format-to-Awareness Map for Static Ad Planning
cards.summary: Use a rough map of static formats by funnel stage to decide which formats to test at the top, middle and bottom of the funnel.
cards.use_when: Building a static ad test plan across funnel stages or filling gaps in a creative testing calendar.
steps: Top of funnel formats: problem agitation statics, native statics, PR/advertorial statics, founder statics (photo of founder doing something, either very curious or very clear).
Middle of funnel formats: comparison ads, before-and-afters, listicles, feature call-outs (where most people default).
Bottom of funnel formats: offer call-outs, reviews, hero product shots.
Note from the source that most people's statics cluster in the middle and bottom, neglecting the top-of-funnel formats that reach cold audiences.
Test across stages rather than only in the account's comfort zone; find which format works, then scale it by rotating a concept element.
Use top-of-funnel formats with long-form primary text or educational landing pages to close the awareness gap.
caveats: Format alone is the least important variable, per the source; the concept (persona, angle, offer) matters more. Do not chase formats without a concept.

cards.title: Diagnosing a Static's Curiosity Direction (Caffeine Gum Example)
cards.summary: A static that sits in the middle—vague enough to be interesting but lacking specificity to sell or clear curiosity—fails at both, and should be pushed to one pole.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a static headline that feels neither clearly persuasive nor deliberately mysterious, or reviewing a static driving to a plain product page.
steps: Check whether the headline is strong enough to convince a cold audience to buy directly; if 'guaranteed energy in just 5 minutes' is all there is, the source judges it insufficient for cold purchase.
Check whether it is vague enough to create a genuine curiosity gap; if not, it is in the middle and will sit as a mid/bottom-funnel attribution ad.
Pick a direction: either add specificity and persuasion to sell cold, or embrace the curiosity gap fully and send the click to an educational listicle or advertorial rather than a product page.
If choosing the curiosity pole, do not try to sell on the landing page itself; the point of the click is education, per the source.
For ads that do create curiosity, avoid the mistake of routing clicks to a standard PDP, which breaks the desire to learn more.
caveats: This is the source's judgment of one ad, used to illustrate the middle-ground failure mode.
Whether a headline is strong enough depends on your product, price and audience.

cards.title: AI-Assisted Static Production with Human Checkpoints
cards.summary: AI can be used at every stage of static production, but automating everything produces slop; keep human intervention at research or concepting, or make the build human.
cards.use_when: Designing an AI-assisted static ad production pipeline for a store that wants volume without losing creative quality.
steps: Choose where to place human intervention rather than automating the whole pipeline; the source's examples of client pipelines place humans at research and concepting.
Option A: fully automate build and variations, but keep research and concepting human.
Option B: use AI-assisted build and research, but keep concepting human (the source calls concepting one of the most important human interventions).
Avoid fully automated feedback loops; pushing ads to an AI for feedback and shipping them without human review produces slop.
Use AI to scrape large datasets for consumer research, and AI generation to speed the build, but keep the winning concept selection human.
If the concept is entirely LLM-generated, everyone gets the same ideas and the edge disappears; feed research context to differentiate but do not rely on it alone.
caveats: The source notes AI can do every step but recommends against full automation; this is advice, not a measured performance result.
Cross-industry idea translation and concept differentiation are areas the source says AI does poorly.

you need enough budget behind ads to reach statistical relevance."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","budgeting","measurement","creative-strategy","experiment-design"]},{"title":"Prioritize Research Over Concepting Over Production","summary":"The static ad production pipeline is research → concepting → build → variations → feedback, and quality collapses if you skip straight to design tools like Canva.","use_when":"Structuring a static ad production workflow or diagnosing why existing statics underperform despite good design.","steps":["Do not open Canva or a template library first; start in a word document or research tool.","Spend roughly 80% of effort on research and concepting, per the source's guidance.","Research means genuinely understanding the consumer, their pain points and their language, not assuming you already know them.","Concept (define persona, angle, offer) only after research is done, then build the static, then vary, then get feedback and launch.","Use AI selectively rather than fully automating every stage; the source recommends human intervention at research or concepting even if build and variations are AI-assisted.","Have AI assist research by scraping large datasets, but keep concepting human because LLM concepting produces the same ideas across everyone.","Recognize that AI struggles to cross-translate peripheral ideas from other industries, which is where human creative differentiation and arbitrage come from."],"caveats":["The 80% figure is the source's recommendation for effort allocation, not a measured finding.","The source notes AI can be used at every stage but warns that automating everything produces slop creative."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","creative-strategy","customer-research","research","static-ads","workflow"]},{"title":"Creative Variation: Change One Concept Element, Not the Pixel","summary":"Because Meta's Andromeda groups near-identical ads, tiny design changes have no measurable uplift; variations should change persona, offer or angle while keeping the winning format.","use_when":"Deciding what to change when scaling a winning static format, or rejecting a designer's background-color variations.","steps":["Define a real variation as a material change to persona, offer or angle; a background color swap or slightly different product pose is not worth testing.","Understand that a color change might produce a 1-2% delta that is statistically unmeasurable without enormous budgets, which the source calls a bad use of spend.","Run tests that are measurable, get meaningful spend behind them, and materially change future creative direction (feeding a creative flywheel).","Treat extremely small variations as wasted because Andromeda will natively group similar ads under the same ad ID and serve them to the same audience.","When scaling a format, substitute a concept element: keep the format and messaging, but swap the product (e.g., greens powder to protein powder) or the persona while holding offer and angle constant.","Use variations only to squeeze a bit more spend through an already-proven concept, not to test whether that concept works."],"caveats":["The source claims Meta introduced this grouping to counter AI-driven ad volume; verify current platform behavior as it may change.","This does not mean format innovation is worthless; a genuinely new format can create temporary first-mover arbitrage."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","creative-strategy","experiment-design","static-ads","measurement","platform"]},{"title":"Expected Gross Profit Per Ad: The Real Comparison Metric","summary":"Compare creative types by expected gross profit after production cost (revenue per ad minus ad spend minus production cost), not by headline ROAS alone.","use_when":"Choosing between producing more statics or more videos in a paid social budget, or justifying a static-heavy creative plan.","steps":["Calculate average revenue per ad unit for each creative type in the account.","Subtract average ad spend per ad (based on the account's actual return, not an idealized one).","Subtract the production cost per ad for that creative type (statics roughly $20, video roughly $200 per the source's example).","Compare the resulting gross profit per ad; the source's illustration shows statics at $880 versus video at $700 at 10x return, and $480 versus $300 at 2x return.","At lower returns, the production-cost gap widens the gross profit difference between cheap and expensive creative.","Use this calculation to prioritize statics for testing and to justify shifting budget toward cheaper creative in lower-ROAS scenarios."],"caveats":["All figures ($1,000 revenue, 10x/2x return, $20/$200 costs) are the source's illustrative examples, not promised outcomes.","ROAS, ad spend and production costs vary widely; plug in your own account numbers."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","budgeting","measurement","static-ads","video","profitability"]},{"title":"Stages of Awareness Applied to Static Ads","summary":"Static ads tend to sit low in the stages of awareness; to scale them you must deliberately build statics for higher awareness stages and use primary text plus landing pages to bridge the gap.","use_when":"Choosing what awareness level a new static ad should target, especially when trying to reach cold audiences instead of retargeting buyers.","steps":["Identify where a proposed static sits on the awareness spectrum: unaware, problem aware, solution aware or most aware.","Recognize the most-aware product-shot static only resonates with people who already know the product and likely visited the site; this is the style 90% of people default to, per the source.","Build solution-aware statics for cold audiences (people who know the problem but not your product).","Place 'problem aware' work higher up the funnel and consider it very cold.","For unaware audiences, use the static image to redirect attention into long-form primary text or an educational landing page; a 4-second static alone cannot teach a problem, a solution and a product.","Pair each static with copy and a landing page at the same stage; mismatched copy and image (e.g., a product-aware image with solution-aware copy) kills performance."],"caveats":["Static ads cannot easily communicate across all awareness stages within one 1080x1080 image; this is a structural limitation, not a design failure.","The '90% of statics' figure is the source's assertion about common practice, not a measured statistic."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","positioning","static-ads","customer-research","landing-page","cold-audience"]},{"title":"Design the Visual Hierarchy on Three Levers","summary":"Control how a viewer's eye moves through a static using sizing, contrast and whitespace so the first fixation lands on the highest-awareness element.","use_when":"Reviewing a static ad layout, or briefing a designer on how the eye should travel through the creative.","steps":["Identify where the viewer's eye lands first (the largest, highest-contrast element) and make sure that element carries the highest-awareness message, not 'protein powder' when it could be 'new technology'.","Recall that sizing directs the eye to the largest element, contrast directs it to whatever differs most, and whitespace redirects attention away from empty space onto the meaningful elements.","Lead the eye through the static in a sequence that pulls the viewer up or through the stages of awareness: high-awareness hook first, then image that creates intrigue, then resolution.","Use the example of a folded powder product: the first headline 'new technology' pulls a broad audience, the clear protein mixing image creates confusion, and subsequent elements resolve it.","Understand that pure design quality is secondary to message clarity, but bad design can destroy authority built by other elements (e.g., poor spacing, off-center product).","Note that design matters most when the static must be non-native and clickbaity, or when it needs to compress an angle, offer and audience into very few words."],"caveats":["The source argues design is not the skill in a static; clarity, messaging and copywriting matter more. Design still matters for framing and authority."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","creative-strategy","static-ads","design","positioning"]},{"title":"Treat Primary Text and Headline as Core, Not Decoration","summary":"On statics, headlines and primary text get far more consumption than on video, so build a YouTube-thumbnail-style curiosity pairing between image and text.","use_when":"Writing the copy that accompanies a static ad image, or reviewing primary text in a static ad breakdown.","steps":["Treat the headline and primary text as equally weighted with the image on statics, because viewers are more likely to read both than on a video ad.","Build a curiosity pairing between image and text like a YouTube thumbnail and title: image raises a question ('what is this mystery powder?'), text adds context without fully resolving it, and the click resolves it.","For native-style statics, keep the image vague (e.g., blurred product) and let the primary text carry the selling.","Check whether the copy matches the awareness stage of the image; a product-aware image paired with solution-aware copy (e.g., a creatine product shot with copy explaining what creatine is) will not work.","For ads with very little text in the image, use long-form primary text to walk the viewer through awareness stages.","Ensure the CTA and primary text support the direction the image set: clickbaity or advertorial images drive a click, native images rely on copy to pull the reader through."],"caveats":["This applies primarily to statics; the source says headline/primary-text consumption is much lower on video ads.","Copy alone cannot rescue a static whose image sits at a mismatched awareness stage."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","copywriting","static-ads","product-page","creative-strategy"]},{"title":"Native vs Non-Native Scroll-Stop Levers","summary":"Statics stop the scroll either by feeling native to the platform or by being deliberately non-native and clickbaity; each direction dictates where the message and selling live.","use_when":"Deciding the creative direction (native organic-feel vs. obvious ad) for a new static before starting design.","steps":["Choose the native route: mimic organic platform content (notepad, text-message, tweet-style formats) so viewers do not register the ad; familiarity stops the scroll and the format gives room to communicate the message.","Choose the interrupt route: make the static dramatically non-native and clickbaity so it is a pattern interrupt; this drives cheap clicks to educational landing pages.","For native statics, plan to carry the selling in long-form primary text and a landing page, since the image gives little away and may not even be recognized as an ad.","For clickbaity or advertorial statics, drive to an educational lander (advertorial, listicle, quiz) rather than a standard product page; do not try to sell directly on the landing page in that direction.","Innovate on format when possible: copied formats only help if you are first to market, but a new working format gives temporary arbitrage."],"caveats":["Model-based native formats can carry brand-safety and legal risk; the source notes blurring brand-identifiable packaging may be advisable but is not certain.","A native static that feels organic still needs the primary text and landing page to do the selling."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","creative-strategy","static-ads","landing-page","copywriting","positioning"]},{"title":"Whitelisting/Native Static with Long-Form Copy (IM8 Example)","summary":"A tweet-style static run from a personality profile, agitating a very wide symptom list and educating on solutions, can reach cold audiences without looking like an ad.","use_when":"Planning a native or whitelisting-style static around a broad symptom/problem list for a supplement or wellness product.","steps":["Run the static from a personality or partner profile (not a brand collaboration) so it feels like organic content and reaches that person's audience.","Lead with a broad problem-agitation list addressed to a very wide audience (e.g., dry eyes, poor vision, low energy, bad skin, fatigue, bleeding gums, painful muscles) to maximize addressable market.","Educate on what each symptom might indicate (e.g., which vitamin deficiency maps to which symptom), then introduce the product as the resolving solution.","Maintain the organic feel by not attaching the brand name to the post.","Keep the primary text long-form, moving the reader from problem to education to product to CTA.","Understand that this static, with a curiosity-building image and hooking long-form copy, typically works well for cold traffic, per the source."],"caveats":["The source calls this its own observation of a live competitor ad, not a guaranteed template.","Whitelisting and personality-page ads carry platform and disclosure considerations; verify current rules."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","static-ads","cold-audience","copywriting","customer-research","whitelisting"]},{"title":"Long-Copy Story Static for Older/Problem-Aware Audiences","summary":"A plain, organic-looking story post with a long narrative about a personal problem can pull a wide audience and disqualify non-relevant viewers through its content.","use_when":"Writing a static ad aimed at an older or problem-aware audience (e.g., menopause, hormonal issues) that needs trust built through story.","steps":["Write the static as if it were an organic Facebook post from an individual, not a brand, to reduce ad recognition.","Open with a line that broadens the audience and creates a mild mystery, then reveal the real topic through the narrative.","Structure the narrative as: protagonist's problem (often affecting relationships), a skeptical attempt at a solution, a 90-day guarantee that lowered the barrier, then the positive outcome.","Use the story to disqualify irrelevant viewers naturally (someone not in the target demographic will scroll past), pre-qualifying the remaining audience.","Explain where the product was found inside the story rather than as a hard sales block.","Follow through to a landing page that matches the story's promised product."],"caveats":["The source shows this as a strong example, not a universal rule; long narrative copy works best with the right audience and offer.","Do not fabricate specific results; the story format is the transferable part, not any claimed outcome."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","static-ads","copywriting","retention","customer-research","positioning"]},{"title":"How Design Quality Conveys or Destroys Authority","summary":"Design alone does not sell, but bad spacing and off-center product shots can erase the authority that specificity and positioning build.","use_when":"Reviewing a finished static for layout quality before it goes live, or deciding whether to fix design versus rewrite copy.","steps":["Check whether design supports or undercuts the authority claims (e.g., a bold specific percentage at the top signals clinical evidence; clunky spacing below it can lose that framing).","Fix basic composition issues: product off-center, poor spacing, inconsistent alignment.","Remove elements that do not earn their space; the source suggests dropping the logo from the static because the brand is visible at the page level.","Replace generic slogans ('you don't have to feel ready, you just have to begin') with concrete features or a review that gives a reason to buy.","Understand that design is not the skill of a static; the messaging, clarity and copywriting are, so do not over-invest in design polish at the expense of the concept.","Use design mainly to control the visual hierarchy and frame, not as a standalone performance lever."],"caveats":["The source's stance is that design 'really doesn't matter' compared to messaging, but also acknowledges design can erode authority—so fix obvious layout problems even if design is secondary."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","static-ads","design","creative-strategy","conversion-optimization"]},{"title":"Match Image and Copy at the Same Awareness Stage","summary":"When the static image assumes one awareness stage and the copy speaks to another, the ad fails; the image and copy must sit at the same stage.","use_when":"Auditing an existing static ad that is underperforming, or QA review before launch.","steps":["Identify the awareness stage the static image assumes (e.g., a product shot means the viewer already knows the product).","Read the primary text and confirm it addresses the same audience; a product-aware image paired with solution-aware copy ('creatine helps you gain strength') will not convert.","When mismatch is found, correct either the image (to match the copy's stage) or the copy (to match the image's stage).","Use a story-based or agitate-based image with copy that speaks to the same problem and audience.","This diagnosis applies to video as well as static: the ad creative and the copy must align to avoid wasted spend."],"caveats":["The creatine example is the source's illustration; stage definitions come from Eugene Schwartz's awareness model referenced by the source."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","creative-strategy","static-ads","conversion-optimization","positioning"]},{"title":"Rotate Concept Elements to Scale a Winning Format","summary":"Once a static format proves out, scale it by substituting a concept element (persona, offer or angle) rather than iterating on the format itself.","use_when":"Planning the next batch of statics after a format like problem-agitation or native advertorial has proven to work.","steps":["Confirm the format is working (e.g., problem agitation, native static, founder static).","Keep the format and messaging structure constant and swap the product (e.g., apply the greens powder static to the protein powder).","Alternatively, keep format, offer and angle and change the persona addressed (e.g., women 30-40 to men).","Alternatively, keep format and persona and change the angle (e.g., weight-loss framing to longevity framing).","Rotate only one element at a time so you can attribute any performance shift to the change.","Avoid the trap of making endless small format tweaks to a single ad; that yields no meaningful new reach or learning."],"caveats":["This is the source's recommended scaling method and assumes the base format retains its performance; results depend on the account and audience.","It does not replace the need to still find new winning concepts, only to multiply the reach of existing ones."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","creative-strategy","static-ads","positioning","offer-design","experiment-design"]},{"title":"Format-to-Awareness Map for Static Ad Planning","summary":"Use a rough map of static formats by funnel stage to decide which formats to test at the top, middle and bottom of the funnel.","use_when":"Building a static ad test plan across funnel stages or filling gaps in a creative testing calendar.","steps":["Top of funnel formats: problem agitation statics, native statics, PR/advertorial statics, founder statics (photo of founder doing something, either very curious or very clear).","Middle of funnel formats: comparison ads, before-and-afters, listicles, feature call-outs (where most people default).","Bottom of funnel formats: offer call-outs, reviews, hero product shots.","Note from the source that most people's statics cluster in the middle and bottom, neglecting the top-of-funnel formats that reach cold audiences.","Test across stages rather than only in the account's comfort zone; find which format works, then scale it by rotating a concept element.","Use top-of-funnel formats with long-form primary text or educational landing pages to close the awareness gap."],"caveats":["Format alone is the least important variable, per the source; the concept (persona, angle, offer) matters more. Do not chase formats without a concept."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","creative-strategy","static-ads","positioning","testing","cold-audience"]},{"title":"Diagnosing a Static's Curiosity Direction (Caffeine Gum Example)","summary":"A static that sits in the middle—vague enough to be interesting but lacking specificity to sell or clear curiosity—fails at both, and should be pushed to one pole.","use_when":"Evaluating a static headline that feels neither clearly persuasive nor deliberately mysterious, or reviewing a static driving to a plain product page.","steps":["Check whether the headline is strong enough to convince a cold audience to buy directly; if 'guaranteed energy in just 5 minutes' is all there is, the source judges it insufficient for cold purchase.","Check whether it is vague enough to create a genuine curiosity gap; if not, it is in the middle and will sit as a mid/bottom-funnel attribution ad.","Pick a direction: either add specificity and persuasion to sell cold, or embrace the curiosity gap fully and send the click to an educational listicle or advertorial rather than a product page.","If choosing the curiosity pole, do not try to sell on the landing page itself; the point of the click is education, per the source.","For ads that do create curiosity, avoid the mistake of routing clicks to a standard PDP, which breaks the desire to learn more."],"caveats":["This is the source's judgment of one ad, used to illustrate the middle-ground failure mode.","Whether a headline is strong enough depends on your product, price and audience."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","static-ads","creative-strategy","copywriting","landing-page","positioning"]},{"title":"AI-Assisted Static Production with Human Checkpoints","summary":"AI can be used at every stage of static production, but automating everything produces slop; keep human intervention at research or concepting, or make the build human.","use_when":"Designing an AI-assisted static ad production pipeline for a store that wants volume without losing creative quality.","steps":["Choose where to place human intervention rather than automating the whole pipeline; the source's examples of client pipelines place humans at research and concepting.","Option A: fully automate build and variations, but keep research and concepting human.","Option B: use AI-assisted build and research, but keep concepting human (the source calls concepting one of the most important human interventions).","Avoid fully automated feedback loops; pushing ads to an AI for feedback and shipping them without human review produces slop.","Use AI to scrape large datasets for consumer research, and AI generation to speed the build, but keep the winning concept selection human.","If the concept is entirely LLM-generated, everyone gets the same ideas and the edge disappears; feed research context to differentiate but do not rely on it alone."],"caveats":["The source notes AI can do every step but recommends against full automation; this is advice, not a measured performance result.","Cross-industry idea translation and concept differentiation are areas the source says AI does poorly."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","static-ads","creative-strategy","automation","workflow","customer-research"]}]}

Static ads are the most undervalued, highest leverage creative type that exists within a Meta account, but most people get them completely wrong. Firstly, statics have the lowest CPMs within creative types. They pretty much always beat videos unless there's a compliance issue. And the best thing about this is that it's the fastest way to test new angles, concepts, offers. You can quickly whip up a new static, you can put it into the account, and you can start testing new concepts. Number two, with the introduction of Andromeda, where creative does the targeting, you want clarity over design. The design of a static ad really doesn't matter. In fact, some of the best static ads that I'm going to show you later in the video, you're going to look at them and go, "How are these converting?" But they've held a quart million dollars in ad spend. And it's because when it comes to statics, you want quick clarity as to what the message is, what the problem is that we're agitating on, and what the solution is. We don't need to go and fuss around with a really nice design. And then lastly, there's three reasons why everyone fails with static ads. Number one, they only run bottom of funnel creative because naturally static ads sit very low down in the stages of awareness. Why is this the case? Why when people think static ads do they think retargeting ad? It's because it's very difficult to communicate through all of the stages of awareness in just one 1080x 1080 static image ad. It's very tough. You don't have many words. you don't have much real estate that you can work with. Whereas in a video, you have way more time. You have infinite more information that you can communicate to the consumer, therefore pulling them through the stages of awareness. So, it is actually very hard to push a static ad up the stages of awareness. And because people don't want to do hard things or because that is a skill that most people don't have, when they make static ads, they just hit a bottom of funnel. They just retarget. Number two is most static ads in most accounts are the exact same thing and there's just a ton of different variation. And I was actually having this conversation with someone the other day where they were saying, "Hey, these two statics we put into the account that we gave to you guys to launch, these are two different concepts." Fundamentally, they are not. They are the exact same concept. They are just a variation. And this is where people can really mess up on static ads is that they think because they have a new design, it's a new concept and it's adding diversity. But the design has nothing to do with broadening out and reaching new audiences. What matters is that you're changing the angle, you're changing the offer, you're changing the persona that you're talking to, or you're changing the format, which is not possible here because we're staying within the constraints of static images. So, you need to change one of these three things. And then the last one is going to be lastclick attribution. And as a byproduct, I'm going to add landing pages in here as well. So if you're running very top offunnel static ads, you will end up driving really cheap CPCs and a lot of traffic to the website that will then end up getting retargeted elsewhere in the account and that will take attribution. And so you'll end up with statics that are spending a lot. The rorowaz might not necessarily be all the way at the profitable return that you want, but the halo effect that it's having on the account is enormous because these high up the funnel static ads normally are some kind of advertorial or native static or longer form creative that needs to drive to an educational lander where they are then pre-educated where a follow-up ad will often get the conversion. And so if you're not using landing pages in your top ofunnel creatives and you're completely reliant on lastclick attribution as your methodology for whether a static ad has worked or not, that is why static ads aren't working for you. Now I want to be very clear. The reason why I'm making this YouTube video is because if you go into YouTube right now and you type how do I make a good static ad or lessons on how to create static ads that are top of funnel and that work on meta ads, they don't exist. All that you will find everywhere when it comes to static ad content is just different formats that you should try. Hey, here's how to make a good static ad on Facebook ads. Try the advertorial format. Try the before and after format. Try this format. That format. Formats fundamentally don't matter. It's the least important of the components as to what creates a good static ad. Purpose of this video is for us to break down to the fundamentals of what makes a good static ad, what makes a bad static ad, and what frameworks do you need to be thinking through when you're creating them, that is content that's actually valuable, because rather than you just copy pasting a bunch of formats that I can give you in this video, which sure I can give you formats all day long, but just follow my Instagram and I post ad reacts on there every day. The idea here is that you can walk away and fundamentally understand how static ads work at their roots so that you can then go and create infinite static ads forever that are actually good and that actually scale. So with that being said, let's dive into the first section of this video, which is why static ads are one of the highest leverage creative types that you have. Number one is the four times cheaper argument. So the argument here is that CPMs are much cheaper on serving static ads, but also creative production is much cheaper. So the reality is is that a good 60 to 90 second video ad in that time that it takes in the resourcing and the expenses to the business, you could probably make four static ads in the same amount of time. Now you could probably make three great static ads if you actually spend a little bit more time ensuring that these are good creative. Now, because of that, there's obviously always going to be a production advantage to statics. Now, this is amplified even further with AI, where AI can help build these statics for you, come up with the concept, and come up with the ideas. So, you can pump out statics if you want for like a dollar a static or less. Now, the reason why most people don't look at this argument and they disregard it straight away is because of the limiting belief that, well, yeah, that's fine, but it's because static sit at the bottom of the funnel and videos sit at the top. And so, sure, we can pump out millions of statics, but if they're sitting at the bottom of funnel, it doesn't matter. And that's correct. If they're sitting at the bottom of funnel, it doesn't matter. But they don't have to. You can make statics that sit higher up the stages of awareness. The second reason why statics are high leverage is because of expected gross profit per ad. Now, what this means is that you take the average ad spend of the ad and you look at the average return and that gives you an expected revenue return per ad unit. So, let's say that on average each ad returns us $1,000 in revenue. Then, what we need to do is minus the ad spend. So let's say these guys are at a 10x return. So we minus $100 in ad spend. And then the final stage here is we want to minus the actual cost of production. What did it cost to make this type of creative? Now with static ads, very cheap. Maybe it's only costing you $20 static ad to make. So then out the back of this, we will have $880 in expected gross profit post production cost. Now, where this becomes interesting is that let's say that you're also putting videos into the account. Videos are also generating you on average $1,000 in revenue per ad. They're also at a 10x return, but a video cost you $200 to make. Now, because of that, the expected gross profit per ad after production cost is actually substantially lower down at $700. Now, this gets a lot more extreme when you start factoring in that the ROI probably isn't at a 10x and you might be running at like, let's say, a 2x. So, it's a $500 advertising cost. And all of a sudden, if we just rerun these gross profit numbers, in this case, you're at 480 GP. In this case, you're down at 300 GP. So this is about 50% less profit or like 30% less profit because statics and videos are returning the same amount assume this is all top of funnel but the cost of production is much lower. Number three is statics are a great testing ground for then moving concepts and ideas over into video format. So, because videos cost so much comparative to producing a static, you can come in and test new angles, new concepts, new personas, new offers in a static ad, see if it performs well, and then if it does, you roll it into higher production shoots that cost more money. This is particularly helpful in offer testing because if your creative is going to sit relatively bottom or middle of funnel and you're not going to make a good high up the stages of awareness static ad, that's fine. You can do offer testing directly here. And so you can directly split test different offers on warm audiences, be able to figure out which converts better, and as a function of that, what the gross profit is off the back of it, and you can continue to nail down the offer. There are three fundamentals of a static ad and what the creative needs to do. Number one, it needs to stop the scroll. Number two, it needs to communicate the message. And number three, it needs to drive action. Now, the reality of all three of these is they end up leading to two real options. When we're thinking about stopping the scroll, there are two ways that you stop people's scroll. either number one the creative feels native within the platform so people don't realize it's an ad and everyone will consume their organic feed or number two it needs to come across super clickbaity or jump out in some way so it's not native at all and it instead becomes a patent interrupt for communicating the message this is where design elements actually become important because you need to communicate normally what the angle is what the offer is and who it is for within the constraints of not many words and not much direction that you can go on the static at. So this is where actually creativity needs to get leveraged the most within a static. But you can also leverage the primary text if you're going to keep the creative relatively native and not have much information in it. Then lastly, you need to drive action. Drive action is also going to lend itself to one of these two things. If it's a super clickbay ad, if it's an avitorial, it's going to naturally drive action because you're going to be insinuating towards some kind of article, some kind of blog on the other side of the click that the user can find out about. If it's a native ad, they're going to be going through long- form copy, which is going to be driving them to action anyway as the copy's pulling them through the stages of awareness. When you're thinking about the hook of a static, another angle that you can come in with is familiarity. This leads into the native static, but you see this a lot in a lot of formats that people choose. So, people will choose stuff like the notepad format or the text message format.
